title: Incense Route
summary: A caravan network carried frankincense and myrrh from southern Arabia to the Mediterranean, passing Petra and ending at ports such as Gaza. Nabataean traders ran it from the 3rd century BC to the 2nd century AD over roughly 1,800 to 2,000 km, and the trade brought wealth to desert towns, including four in the Negev.

uncertainty.note: Dates are those of the Nabataean trade in the Negev nomination (3rd century BC to 2nd century AD). Livius reports frankincense use and dromedary caravans from earlier centuries, so the wider route is older than this span.

as_recorded.value: From the 3rd century BC until 2nd century AD, the Nabateans transported frankincense and myrrh across the desert from Arabia to the Mediterranean coast, a distance of some 1,800 km

where.modern_name: Petra, Jordan (central station; the route runs from Shabwa, Yemen to Gaza)
where.historical_name: Nabataean Petra, a station between south Arabia and the Mediterranean ports; Shabwa was capital of Hadramaut

waypoints.label: Shabwa, capital of Hadramaut: Pliny counts sixty-five stations between Shabwa and Gaza.
Najran: caravans went to the oasis of Najran after the capitals of Qataban and Saba.
Petra, capital of the Nabataeans, about 500 km north of the Hegra and Dedan stages. Point is Al-Khazneh, Petra.

waypoints.date: 3rd century BC to 2nd century AD (Israel nomination)
waypoints.label: Gaza: Mediterranean end of the route; ports named by Livius include Gaza.

importance.justification: Long-distance caravan network that supplied the Hellenistic-Roman world with frankincense and enriched the desert towns along it.

beats.caption: Frankincense and myrrh from Oman, Yemen and Somalia travel north by caravan through Shabwa and Najran toward Petra and Gaza.
Nabataean carriers move the resins some 1,800 km to the Mediterranean, and Negev towns live off the trade for five centuries.
Roman occupation of Petra ends Nabataean control, and the frankincense trade shifts to routes more profitable for the Romans.

reviewer_note: Least sure: route waypoints are undated stages from Livius (Pliny), not dated visits; Timna, Marib, Hegra and Dedan are omitted. Id year -1000 comes from the queue; the sourced span is 3rd century BC to 2nd century AD. UNESCO pages were blocked, so the Israeli nomination dossier (which reproduces the ICOMOS text) is the main source.
